text: Blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration is favored by molecules with low TPSA (<90 Å²), moderate LogP (1-3), and MW < 450 Da.
High lipophilicity (LogP > 3) and low polar surface area enhance passive diffusion across the BBB.
Molecules with hydrogen bond donors (HBD) > 3 typically have poor BBB penetration due to reduced membrane permeability.
P-glycoprotein (P-gp) substrates are actively effluxed from the brain; avoid recognition motifs to improve BBB penetration.
Basic amines with pKa 7-10 can cross the BBB via ion trapping mechanism.
Small, lipophilic molecules without charged groups at physiological pH are good BBB penetrators.
Aromatic rings and halogen substituents generally favor BBB penetration by increasing lipophilicity.
Carboxylic acids and sulfonamides typically have poor BBB penetration due to ionization at pH 7.4.
Nitro-aromatic scaffolds often correlate with hepatotoxicity via reactive metabolites and oxidative stress.
Lipophilic molecules with TPSA < 50 Å² frequently cross the BBB and may trigger CNS side effects including dizziness and sedation.
Sulfonamide motifs can induce hypersensitivity reactions; monitor immune-related adverse events like skin rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
High molecular weight compounds (>500 Da) often have poor oral bioavailability and may accumulate, causing chronic toxicity.
Molecules with multiple hydrogen bond donors (>5) may have renal excretion issues and nephrotoxicity risk.
Compounds with LogP > 5 tend to accumulate in adipose tissue and may cause metabolic disorders or prolonged half-life effects.
Aromatic amines can form reactive metabolites through N-oxidation, potentially causing genotoxicity and carcinogenicity.
Quinolone antibiotics are associated with tendon disorders, QT prolongation, and CNS effects.
Fluorinated compounds may have extended half-lives and potential thyroid disruption effects.
Polycyclic aromatic structures increase the risk of phototoxicity and skin sensitization.
Compounds with reactive functional groups (aldehydes, Michael acceptors) may cause protein adduct formation and idiosyncratic toxicity.
Beta-lactam antibiotics can cause allergic reactions ranging from mild rash to severe anaphylaxis.
Drugs with high plasma protein binding may have drug-drug interactions and displacement effects.
Statins are associated with muscle-related adverse events including myalgia and rhabdomyolysis.
NSAIDs can cause gastrointestinal bleeding, renal impairment, and cardiovascular events.
Compounds with low TPSA (<20 Å²) and high LogP may cause membrane disruption and general cytotoxicity.
Hydroxamic acids are often associated with bone marrow suppression and hematological toxicity.
Drugs metabolized by CYP3A4 are prone to drug interactions with common inhibitors like grapefruit juice.
Compounds with multiple chiral centers may have different toxicity profiles for each stereoisomer.
Phosphate-containing drugs may cause electrolyte imbalances and mineral metabolism disorders.
SIDER side effects are organized by System Organ Class (SOC): Hepatobiliary disorders often linked to reactive metabolites and oxidative stress.
SIDER SOC: Nervous system disorders include dizziness, headache, somnolence; often correlated with BBB penetration (low TPSA, high LogP).
SIDER SOC: Gastrointestinal disorders (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) are common with oral drugs and irritants.
SIDER SOC: Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders include rash, pruritus, urticaria; often immune-mediated.
SIDER SOC: Cardiac disorders (arrhythmia, QT prolongation) linked to ion channel interactions, especially hERG.
SIDER SOC: Renal and urinary disorders include nephrotoxicity, often from accumulation or direct tubular damage.
SIDER SOC: Musculoskeletal disorders (myalgia, arthralgia) associated with statins and fluoroquinolones.
SIDER SOC: Psychiatric disorders (anxiety, depression, insomnia) linked to CNS-active compounds.
SIDER SOC: Blood and lymphatic system disorders include anemia, thrombocytopenia; monitor with cytotoxic agents.
SIDER SOC: Immune system disorders range from mild hypersensitivity to severe anaphylaxis; sulfonamides and beta-lactams are common triggers.
SIDER SOC: Eye disorders (blurred vision, dry eyes) may occur with anticholinergic drugs.
SIDER SOC: Respiratory disorders (dyspnea, cough) can be drug-induced, especially with ACE inhibitors.
SIDER SOC: Metabolism and nutrition disorders include weight changes, appetite loss, electrolyte imbalances.
SIDER SOC: Vascular disorders (hypotension, hypertension, flushing) related to vasoactive compounds.
SIDER SOC: General disorders (fatigue, fever, pain) are non-specific but frequently reported.
Carboxylic acid groups often associated with gastrointestinal irritation and potential ulceration.
Amide bonds are generally stable but can be hydrolyzed in vivo; monitor for active metabolites.
Primary amines may undergo oxidative deamination; secondary amines are often more stable.
Hydroxyl groups increase water solubility but may be sites for glucuronidation and rapid clearance.
Heteroaromatic rings (pyridine, thiophene) can interact with CYP enzymes and affect drug metabolism.
Halogen substituents (Cl, Br, I) increase lipophilicity and may affect metabolic stability.
Tox21 NR-AR: Androgen receptor agonists/antagonists affect male reproductive function and muscle development. Compounds with steroid-like scaffolds often show AR activity.
Tox21 NR-AR-LBD: Androgen receptor ligand-binding domain assay detects direct AR binding. Phenolic and hydroxyl-substituted aromatics may show activity.
Tox21 NR-ER: Estrogen receptor activity is associated with endocrine disruption. Bisphenols, parabens, and phenolic compounds often bind ER.
Tox21 NR-ER-LBD: Estrogen receptor ligand-binding domain assay. Compounds with planar aromatic rings and hydroxyl groups at specific positions mimic estradiol.
Tox21 NR-AhR: Aryl hydrocarbon receptor activation is linked to dioxin-like toxicity, immune suppression, and carcinogenicity. Polyhalogenated aromatics are potent AhR agonists.
Tox21 NR-Aromatase: Aromatase inhibition affects estrogen biosynthesis. Triazole and imidazole antifungals are known aromatase inhibitors.
Tox21 NR-PPAR-gamma: PPAR-gamma modulates glucose and lipid metabolism. Thiazolidinediones and certain fatty acid derivatives activate this receptor.
Tox21 SR-ARE: Antioxidant response element activation indicates oxidative stress response via Nrf2 pathway. Electrophilic compounds and Michael acceptors activate ARE.
Tox21 SR-ATAD5: ATAD5 pathway activation indicates DNA damage response. Genotoxic compounds, alkylating agents, and intercalators trigger this pathway.
Tox21 SR-HSE: Heat shock response element activation indicates protein misfolding stress. Heavy metals, arsenicals, and proteotoxic compounds activate HSE.
Tox21 SR-MMP: Mitochondrial membrane potential disruption indicates mitochondrial toxicity. Uncouplers, protonophores, and respiratory chain inhibitors affect MMP.
Tox21 SR-p53: p53 pathway activation indicates DNA damage and potential carcinogenicity. Compounds causing strand breaks or crosslinks activate p53.
Nuclear receptors (NRs) are ligand-activated transcription factors. Small lipophilic molecules with planar aromatic cores and hydrogen bonding groups often show NR activity.
Stress response pathways (SR) in Tox21 detect cellular damage mechanisms. Electrophilic compounds often activate multiple stress pathways including ARE, p53, and MMP.
Endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs) interfere with hormone signaling via NR-ER, NR-AR, or aromatase. Phenolic compounds and plasticizers are common EDCs.
Nitroaromatic compounds often activate SR-p53 and SR-ATAD5 due to their genotoxic potential via nitroreduction to reactive intermediates.
Quinones and hydroquinones can cause oxidative stress (SR-ARE activation) and mitochondrial toxicity (SR-MMP) through redox cycling.
Heavy metals (Cd, Pb, Hg, As) activate multiple Tox21 stress pathways including SR-HSE, SR-ARE, and SR-MMP due to protein binding and oxidative damage.
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are potent NR-AhR agonists and potential carcinogens. Planar, lipophilic structures enhance AhR binding.
Organophosphates may show Tox21 activity through off-target nuclear receptor effects beyond their primary acetylcholinesterase inhibition.
